title: Three Lenses, Layer by Layer
takeaway: Placed side by side on the same six prompts, the three lenses fail in opposite directions: the logit lens prints uninterpretable fragments below roughly layer 58, and the tuned lens prints the eventual answer from about layer 38 onward, while the J-lens is the only column that shows the intermediate steps in the middle layers. All three agree in the last few layers, where each simply reports the next token.
walkthrough:
This item is a live widget rather than a printed panel. It holds six prompts, each with three parallel columns of readouts, one per lens: the [[jacobian-lens]], the [[logit-lens]] and the [[tuned-lens]]. Each row is one layer, and each cell prints only that lens's top-1 token there. Hovering a cell opens its top-10. The rows run from the early middle of the network to the final layer. The paper names no model; its default subject is Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

The three lenses differ only in what is applied to the [[residual-stream]] before the [[unembedding-matrix]]. The logit lens applies nothing. The J-lens inserts a corpus-averaged Jacobian, so a cell names a token the activation disposes the model to say ([[verbalizable-representation]]). The tuned lens inserts a per-layer affine map trained to match the model's output distribution.

The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers and reindexes them to 0-100, so a label reads as a percentage of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The band from roughly 38 to roughly 92 is the [[workspace-layers]] range.

### Reading down a column

In the last few layers all three columns say the same thing, the model's [[next-token-prediction]] — the paper's motor regime ([[motor-layers]]). The differences sit earlier.

The [[multihop-benchmark]] prompt is the clearest case. The J-lens column runs color in the early workspace layers, then Mars, then red. The logit-lens column carries Mars and red over the same upper layers, but below layer 58 it prints fragments — vah, valea, general — that do not read as anything.

The other prompts repeat this. On the [[multilingual-benchmark]] prompt both lenses surface opposite, then big or large, then 大, and only the J-lens recovers Chinese, one layer earlier. On the mental-arithmetic prompt ([[order-of-operations-benchmark]]) both surface nine and then seven, and only the J-lens adds arithmetic and math in earlier layers. On the fluorescent-protein and ASCII-face prompts the J-lens column reads as a coherent sequence while the logit-lens column is largely noise throughout.

The tuned-lens column fails differently. It does not go noisy; it goes early. On the multihop prompt it prints red from layer 38 onward. On the multilingual prompt it prints 大. On the fluorescent-protein prompt it prints the next letter of the sequence, and on the [[poetry-benchmark]] and ASCII-face prompts it prints whitespace. The intermediates are not always absent — Mars, big and nine do appear at lower ranks in some layers — but the output prediction crowds them out of rank 1.

Two hedges come with the figure. Below the workspace onset the J-lens is noisy too, much like the logit lens. And the authors state that the logit lens captures much of the same workspace content where it works, and remains a very useful tool in practice.

terms.definition: The paper's readout technique: a corpus-averaged Jacobian for each layer is composed with the unembedding, giving every vocabulary token a score against a residual-stream activation. One of the three columns per prompt.

The earlier technique the J-lens corrects: the final unembedding is applied directly to the intermediate residual stream, which amounts to setting the Jacobian to the identity. One of the three columns per prompt.

A related technique that trains a per-layer affine map so that its readout matches the model's final output distribution. The third column per prompt, and the one the paper argues is optimized for the wrong target.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token in a lens's ranked list at one layer. Every cell in the figure prints one of these and nothing else.

The widget's interaction: hovering a cell expands it from the top-1 token to the ten highest-scoring tokens at that layer, which is where lower-ranked intermediates such as Mars in the tuned-lens column become visible.
Depth in the network. The paper samples 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and reindexes them to 0-100, so a layer label is a percentage of total depth rather than an absolute layer count.
The middle band, roughly layer 38 to layer 92, in which the paper argues the J-space carries persistent abstract content. The intermediates discussed here appear in this band.
The final few layers, where lens vectors track the imminent output rather than intermediate computation. This is where all three columns converge on the same token.

Roughly the first third of depth, before the workspace onset. The figure's rows start after the early middle of the network, and the text notes that below the workspace the J-lens is noisy much as the logit lens is.
A two-hop factual question whose answer requires computing a bridging entity that is never stated, for example the color of the planet fourth from the Sun.
The J-lens top-1 tokens down the multihop column: the topic of the question in the early workspace layers, then the unspoken bridging entity, then the answer.
The fragments the logit lens prints below layer 58 on the multihop prompt. The paper names them as examples of readouts that carry no interpretable content.
A prompt written entirely in a non-English language, used to test whether the model routes its computation through English-aligned representations before producing the non-English answer.
Top-1 tokens both the J-lens and the logit lens surface on the multilingual prompt: the relation being asked for, then the English equivalent of the answer.
The Chinese character for "big", the model's actual output on the multilingual prompt. It appears at the top of all three columns in the later layers, and in the tuned-lens column much earlier.

The token naming the output language, which the paper reports only the J-lens recovers, and one layer earlier than the shared tokens. The prompt never names the language, so its presence indicates detection rather than copying.
An arithmetic expression whose correct evaluation requires a partial result before the remaining operation is applied.
The two number words both the J-lens and the logit lens surface on the mental-arithmetic prompt, in that order down the layers.
Task-naming tokens the J-lens surfaces in the layers below the numeric intermediates on the mental-arithmetic prompt, and which the logit lens does not surface.

A prompt presenting a raw amino-acid sequence, on which the J-lens reads a coherent sequence of intermediates while the logit lens is largely noise. One of the two prompts where the paper says the gap is starkest.
A prompt containing a face drawn in ASCII characters. The second prompt where the J-lens reads a coherent sequence and the logit lens does not.

A rhyming couplet with the lens read at the newline between the two lines, where the word of interest is the second line's planned final word. The next token at that position is a newline, which is why a lens biased toward the output surfaces whitespace.
What the tuned lens prints on the poetry and ASCII-face prompts: the literal next token at those readout positions, in place of any intermediate.

terms.term: next letter of the protein sequence
terms.definition: What the tuned lens prints on the fluorescent-protein prompt: the upcoming amino-acid character, which is the correct next token and carries no information about the protein's identity.
The per-position vector each layer reads from and writes to. Every cell in the figure is computed from the residual stream at one layer and one position.
The final linear map from the residual stream to vocabulary scores. All three lenses end in it; they differ only in what they apply before it.
The Claude model the paper reports results on by default. The figure does not state its model, so this is the paper's stated default rather than a label in the item.
A representation poised to be put into words should the occasion arise. This is what a J-lens cell names, as distinct from a prediction of the immediate next token.
The paper's broader framework for setting the three lenses against each other; this figure is its qualitative half, with the quantitative half reported separately.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompts shown. The paper says they were chosen to illustrate the two failure modes it describes: logit-lens degradation in earlier layers, and the tuned lens skipping ahead to the output.
Columns per prompt, one for each lens: J-lens, logit lens, tuned lens.
How many tokens each cell prints. Restricting each cell to the single top token is what makes the three columns directly comparable at a glance.
How many tokens a hovered cell reveals. The paper uses this depth of readout to note that Mars, big and nine do appear in the tuned lens at lower ranks, rather than being absent.

The paper's reporting convention: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, reindexed so that a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. Consecutive sampled layers therefore sit about 4 apart on the 0-100 scale.
The depth below which the logit lens produces uninterpretable fragments on the multihop prompt. Above it, the logit lens tracks Mars and red alongside the J-lens.

The layer from which the tuned lens already prints red on the multihop prompt. It is also the layer at which the paper's separate measurements place the workspace onset, so the tuned lens is reporting the answer from the moment there is anything to report.
The approximate end of the workspace band in the paper's layer indexing. Above it the readouts pass into the motor regime, where all three lenses agree.
How much earlier the J-lens recovers Chinese than the shared tokens on the multilingual prompt. Given 25 sampled layers on a 0-100 scale, one sampled layer is about 4 percent of depth.

The two numeric readouts on the mental-arithmetic prompt, surfaced in that order by both the J-lens and the logit lens. The paper reports the order down the layers but does not print the expression that produces them.
The version of the Sonnet model the paper reports on by default. Key results are corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5, though this particular figure names no model.
